channel.title: Acme: Daily Reading List
channel.description: Noteworthy articles from across the web.

item.title: Books may get an ‘organic’ human-authored stamp
item.description: British startup Books by People won approval for a thumbprint-style mark identifying human-authored books. Its process combines declarations, manuscript checks and review of drafts and research. Five publishers have joined, though critics warn that certification could wrongly cast suspicion on writers.

item.title: Turkish publisher wins a second freedom-to-publish award
item.description: The Association of American Publishers honored Avesta Publishing House for defending Kurdish literature and culture despite book bans, a burned warehouse and a website shutdown. Founded in 1995, Avesta also received the award in 2005 and has published hundreds of books on marginalized histories.

item.title: Betty Boop, Blondie and classic detectives join the public domain
item.description: The 2026 public-domain class opened U.S. reuse of works from 1930, including early Betty Boop and Blondie appearances, Nancy Drew, Sam Spade and Miss Marple. Also newly free are “The Maltese Falcon,” “As I Lay Dying,” “Animal Crackers,” “I Got Rhythm” and “Georgia on My Mind,” with later character elements still protected.

item.title: WordPress 7.1.3 fixes seven security flaws
item.description: WordPress 7.1.3 is a maintenance and security release with seven security fixes and four bug fixes. The patched issues include stored cross-site scripting, denial of service, second-order SQL injection in WXR export and disclosure of comments on private or unpublished posts. Site owners are urged to update immediately.

item.title: MacKenzie Scott’s serialized dystopia tests self-publishing
item.description: Rhoda Feng examines MacKenzie Scott’s decision to serialize a dystopian third novel on Substack rather than use a traditional publisher. The essay treats the experiment as both a possible protest against Amazon and evidence of how thoroughly Kindle-era genre fiction, direct publishing and platform economics have reshaped the novel.

item.title: St. Augustine’s colonial archaeology goes online
item.description: The Florida Museum’s Interactive Digital St. Augustine database opens artifacts from colonial household sites to researchers and the public. Built with the Digital Archaeological Archive of Comparative Slavery, the project starts with three excavated lots and makes part of a million-object collection searchable online.

item.title: A database expert gets Doom running almost entirely in SQL
item.description: Lukas Vogel rebuilt Doom’s game logic inside a Postgres-compatible database using 5,900 lines of SQL. A 1,300-line renderer spans 89 tables, while a small Python front end handles input, sound and display. The relational approach even makes multiplayer synchronization and live changes to weapons or enemies unusually natural.

item.title: Six-year project fully decompiles Super Smash Bros. Melee
item.description: A preservation team has converted the 2001 GameCube classic into C code that compiles to a byte-for-byte match of the original executable. The result exposes the engine, physics and game mechanics for study and could support future ports and mods, though users still need legally obtained game assets.

item.title: WordPress reorganizes its core maintainers and bug gardeners
item.description: WordPress refreshed its lists of component maintainers and bug gardeners, then created GitHub teams with triage access for those contributors and experienced Gutenberg developers. The practical goal is clearer ownership and easier pull-request review, labeling and assignment across the core project.

item.title: Minecraft Java Edition sheds its code obfuscation
item.description: Minecraft Java Edition 26.1 no longer obscures its executable code and now requires Java 25. The change should make the game easier for modders to inspect, debug and extend, although Mojang emphasizes that readable code is not the same as open-source or freely licensed code.

item.title: Basil Wolverton’s grotesque visions of Revelation
item.description: A look at the strange religious art of Basil Wolverton, whose famously lumpy “spaghetti and meatball” cartoon style also produced stark illustrations of Revelation. The piece connects the creator of Lena the Hyena and MAD grotesques to a less familiar, deeply serious body of work.

item.title: Boston opens 135 years of historic newspapers as data
item.description: Boston Public Library and Harvard released an open dataset drawn from 1.47 million newspaper pages published from 1795 to 1930. It contains 16.3 billion words across 73 languages, plus an open-source processing pipeline that other libraries and archives can adapt.

item.title: Duke maps the riches—and limits—of the 2026 public domain
item.description: Duke’s annual guide catalogs works from 1930 now free to use in the U.S., including early Betty Boop, Blondie, Nancy Drew and Sam Spade, plus films, songs and art. It also explains the archaeology behind the dates: only the original 1930 versions are newly public, while later adaptations and trademarks can still impose limits.
item.source: Duke Center for the Study of the Public Domain

item.title: Apache XMLBeans 5.4.1 ships with fixes and packaging cleanup
item.description: Apache has released XMLBeans 5.4.1, the Java library that binds XML schemas to generated Java types while also supporting DOM, cursors and schema reflection. The maintenance release brings bug fixes and packaging cleanup—a useful update for Java projects that still need rigorous, schema-aware XML processing.

item.title: Six new voices make the 4thWrite short-story shortlist
item.description: The 10th 4thWrite prize has shortlisted six unpublished writers of color whose stories range from office comedy and friendship to grief and dystopian London. The winner receives £1,000, a publishing workshop and publication in The Guardian, continuing a competition that has helped launch several writing careers.
